title: The anchoress's window
hookLine: Julian lived through plague and revolt, and gave counsel through a window to passers-by

cards: A woman from the town of Lynn has come to stand outside a church in Norwich. She is restless, loud in her weeping, and not everyone trusts her.
She has visions, she says, and she wants to know whether they come from God or from somewhere else. She doesn't knock on a door.

She goes to a window in the wall of a small cell built onto the church, and speaks to the woman inside, who will never come out. The visitor is Margery Kempe. The woman behind the window is the one we call Julian.

teach.h: OUTSIDE THE WALL: PLAGUE AND UPRISING.
teach.b: On day two hundred seventy-one we met Julian in her cell, and the visions she wrote down.

Today, look the other way, out through the window toward the street. Julian's world wasn't quiet. She lived, tradition says, through years of plague and uprising, when angry crowds marched and the powerful struck back.
All of that went on outside her wall, and people came to her window carrying it. We know of one visit because Margery Kempe told it in her own book.
Margery describes talking with Julian over several days, pouring out her visions, her tears, the things God seemed to be asking of her. Julian's answer, as Margery remembers it, is careful and kind.
Paraphrased: test these stirrings by whether they lead you toward the love of God and of your neighbor.
The Holy Spirit never moves anyone against charity. Be patient, and don't be shaken by what people say about you.

That echoes the First Letter of John, in the King James Bible: "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God". Julian didn't tell Margery she was a saint, or a fraud.
She gave her a way to tell for herself. And notice what the window asked of Julian. She couldn't go out and fix anyone's life; she could only listen, and answer.
Proverbs puts the other side plainly: "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him." At the window, hearing came first.

how: Christians in several traditions seek out spiritual direction, a regular conversation with an experienced listener about prayer and life, and Julian is sometimes remembered as an early example of that kind of counsel.

games.q: at the anchoress's window — tap the pairs.

s: an anchoress saw no one at all
Julian's cell had a window to the street, and people came to her for counsel.
Margery Kempe's own book tells of visiting Julian
Margery describes talking with her over several days.
Julian told Margery whether she was a saint or a fraud
she gave her a test instead: the Holy Spirit never moves anyone against charity.

games.q: you're Julian. a restless visitor at your window pours out visions and tears, and asks whether they come from God. what do you say?
o: tell her she's clearly a saint.
tell her she's imagining it and should go home.
give her a way to test it: does it lead to love of God and neighbor?
games.why: as Margery remembers it, Julian told her the Holy Spirit never moves anyone against charity, and to be patient.

practice: Choose one person who might need to talk, a friend going through something, a relative whose calls you let ring, and imagine listening the way Julian did: not fixing, not jumping in, hearing the whole thing.
Notice where you'd usually interrupt, and let that urge pass. If you pray, hold them in prayer; if not, hold their voice in mind.
